title: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover

reading.body:
This is a case of an automated alert being acted on as if it were a confirmed identification. A Flock Safety license plate reader misread the first letter of Steven Melvin's plate and matched his BMW to a similar stolen vehicle, and the match was treated as grounds for a stop. The failure sits at the handoff between the system's output and enforcement: the reader produced a candidate match, and the response was an armed detention lasting more than five minutes rather than a check of the plate itself.

Flock's own position, stated after the incident, is that its alerts should be independently verified before enforcement. That verification is the step that would have caught the error, since the misread was in a single character of the plate and the vehicle was only similar to the stolen one, not the same. The sheriff's office attributed the malfunction to an illegal tinted plate cover, which places the system outside the conditions it was built to read under, and it found the deputy's actions reasonable.

What is not established is whether the plate cover was in fact illegal or in fact caused the misread, since both claims come from the sheriff's office rather than from an independent finding. No ruling on the detention is reported, and the account of the malfunction is an official explanation rather than a verified cause.

reports.title: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover

summary: Steven Melvin, age 42, of York County, South Carolina, was reportedly detained at gunpoint for more than five minutes after a Flock Safety automated license plate reader misidentified the first letter of his plate and matched his BMW to a similar stolen vehicle. The sheriff’s office later said an illegal tinted plate cover caused the malfunction and found the deputy’s actions reasonable. Flock said alerts should be independently verified before enforcement.
